what_it_does: Many small embedded devices — think tiny environmental sensors or wearable health monitors — harvest energy from their surroundings (solar, vibration, radio waves) and run only when enough energy has accumulated; they may lose power at any moment. To survive those power cuts, they use non-volatile memory (NVM — memory that keeps its contents without power) as their main storage. The catch is a subtle data-hazard called Write After Read (WAR): if a program reads a value from NVM into a fast temporary cache, modifies it in the cache, but then gets interrupted before writing the new value back, a restart could see a stale value in NVM. Existing systems detect this by keeping a separate tracking structure alongside the cache, which adds complexity and overhead. NACHO integrates WAR detection directly into the cache controller itself — the hardware that manages what lives in the cache — so no separate tracker is needed. Because the cache now catches hazards early, the system checkpoints (takes a snapshot of its state) much less often, which means fewer energy-costly writes to NVM and faster overall operation.
